name: Crystal deodorant (alum stone)

image.caption: okra, yuzu and crystal body deodorant

lead: An alum stone is a simple, fragrance-free deodorant: rub it on damp underarms or feet for fresher skin, with no scent or added ingredients.

It is a block of potassium or ammonium alum, an astringent described as inhibiting the bacterial action that causes odor. It does not block sweat like antiperspirants. Alum has been used since antiquity, and powdered potassium alum (tawas) is a traditional deodorant in Island Southeast Asia. No controlled trials of effectiveness were found.

paras: The stone is wetted and swiped over underarms or feet, usually daily, and often chosen as a natural alternative to conventional deodorants.

Case reports describe irritant dermatitis and granulomatous dermatitis in the armpits. Alum is an aluminium compound, though chemically different from antiperspirant salts, so aluminium-free marketing is not exact.

news.title: Natural crystal deodorant is not aluminum - free

chain: Alum salt rubbed on damp skin
angle.text: Alum stones are rubbed on damp skin as a natural, fragrance-free deodorant, with use going back to antiquity. The published literature is mostly case reports of skin reactions; no controlled trials of odor control were found.

lead: Crystal deodorant, often sold as an alum stone or "rock crystal", is a block of potassium or ammonium alum, a hydrated double sulfate salt of aluminium, rubbed on damp skin to reduce underarm and foot odour.[1][2] For appearance and grooming it offers a fragrance-free way to stay odour-free without scent or antiperspirant ingredients, which is why it appears in men's grooming and gym-culture discussions as a simple, low-cost option.[3][4]

Alum has been used since antiquity, as a dye mordant, a water clarifier and a styptic for shaving nicks, and in the Philippines and Island Southeast Asia powdered potassium alum (tawas) is a traditional scentless deodorant.[2] Although sometimes marketed as aluminium-free, alum is an aluminium compound, chemically different from the aluminium salts used in antiperspirants.[1]

Published literature on the products consists mainly of case reports of skin reactions, including irritant dermatitis and granulomatous dermatitis.[5][6] No controlled trials of effectiveness were found.
infobox: Potassium or ammonium alum, KAl(SO4)2 or similar[2]
Styptic for shaving nicks, water clarification[2][15]

paras: Alum is a group of hydrated double sulfates, with potassium alum the form usually meant. It dissolves in water, tastes astringent and acts as a mild acid.[2] Deodorant stones are usually used as a solid block moistened with water and swiped over skin, while powdered or liquid forms also exist; patents from the 1990s describe a rotating-base tube for dispensing solid crystal deodorant and a liquid form made by dissolving alum in water or water and ethanol.[7][8]

Body odour arises when skin bacteria break down the oily secretions of the apocrine glands in the armpits and groin, so products that act on bacteria are distinct from antiperspirants that reduce sweat.[1] Wikipedia describes crystal deodorants as inhibiting bacterial action and as popular "natural" products; they do not plug sweat ducts in the way antiperspirant aluminium salts are described to.[1]

Herodotus mentioned Egyptian alum as a valuable trade good, and Pliny the Elder and Dioscorides described it by its astringent properties. It was the most common mordant in medieval Islamic dye industries, and Louis Vauquelin showed in 1797 that common alum is a double salt.[2] Britain banned its use in bread in 1758.[2]

Commercial deodorants arrived later: Wikipedia dates the first modern product, Mum, to an 1888 patent, with antiperspirants following from 1903 and a 1941 patent that reduced irritation from aluminium chloride formulas.[1] Crystal deodorant products emerged as a natural alternative in the late twentieth century, and US patents for a liquid alum deodorant (1994) and a tube dispenser for solid crystals (1996) reflect that commercial interest.[7][8]

sections.h: Use in grooming and gym culture
paras: On T Nation, a bodybuilding and strength forum, members have discussed crystal deodorant since the mid-2000s. One 2006 poster described a roughly five-dollar stone as lasting about a year as a back-to-basics alternative to commercial products, and another described it as an odourless, opaque stone wetted at the sink and used like ordinary deodorant.[4][3]

Some posters report using it on the chest and back for sweat smell in summer, while another found it ineffective alone and recommended combining it with another product; another poster said it was the only product that lasted all day without irritation.[9][10] A further thread repeats the idea that the product works by killing the bacteria responsible for odour.[11] Reports are individual and mixed, and one poster recounted a friend who found no benefit.[12]

A 1999 report in Cutis described two patients who developed irritant dermatitis of the underarms shortly after using an over-the-counter natural deodorant crystal containing alum, calling it a previously unreported reaction to an ancient agent with newfound popularity as an alternative health product.[5] A 2014 report in the International Journal of Dermatology described crystal deodorant-induced axillary granulomatous dermatitis.[6] Wikipedia notes a 1999 study finding synthetic potassium alum a weak skin irritant.[1]

The US FDA's 2003 review found insufficient data to change the status of aluminium antiperspirants.[1] The National Cancer Institute states there is no scientific evidence linking antiperspirants or deodorants to breast cancer, while noting research is conflicting and more studies are needed; a 2014 review found little evidence that aluminium exposure raises Alzheimer's risk.[13][1] These statements concern antiperspirants generally; no source examined alum stones specifically.

A separate hygiene issue is shared use. A 2011 laboratory study in Pakistan, where barbers commonly rub potash alum stones on shaving cuts, reported that hepatitis C virus RNA remained detectable after treatment of infected blood with alum, and the authors argued for banning shared alum stones on shaving cuts at barber shops.[14] That study concerns shared stones on broken skin rather than personal deodorant use.

Alum has been used as a flocculant in water treatment, and a 2017 Colombian study evaluated a rural filtration prototype that used alum stone in its clarification stage, reporting 99.9 percent reductions in coliforms and 98 percent in turbidity.[15] Alum also serves as a styptic for shaving nicks, a food additive and a tanning agent.[2]
No controlled studies of effectiveness were found. Published human data consist of case reports of irritant and granulomatous dermatitis following use.[5][6]

lore.intro: In strength and grooming forums, crystal deodorant is discussed as a cheap, long-lasting, unscented option, with enthusiastic and sceptical reports side by side.[4][9]
